name: Hawk
description: Telescopic fovea resolves at 8x human acuity, detecting prey from 3 km. Peregrine stoop reaches 389 km/h with real-time aerodynamic calculation. Dual fovea: forward telescopic + lateral wide-field. UV tetrachromatic vision reveals prey urine trails.

core_attributes.neurology: dual-fovea retina, tetrachromatic UV vision, rapid motor cortex
core_attributes.pattern: telescopic precision targeting, ballistic dive geometry, dual-fovea scanning

scope.definition: Strike accuracy of red-tailed hawk — fraction of stoops (dives) resulting in prey contact within 5 cm of initial target point — from high-speed video in field and falconry studies.

evidence.source: Tucker (2000) 'The deep fovea, sideways vision, and spiral flight paths in raptors', Journal of Experimental Biology 203:3745-3754; Frost (2010) raptor predation accuracy surveys.
cross_domain_examples: peregrine falcon strike accuracy 0.85-0.95 on moving targets from 300 m altitude dive
dual fovea provides simultaneous frontal binocular and lateral monocular fields for target lock
guided missile terminal phase: 0.92 accuracy in non-maneuvering target scenario — engineered analogue

scope.falsifiability: If hawk strike success rates on equivalent prey types fall below 0.70 in controlled behavioral studies, the high-accuracy targeting model overstates true precision.
scope.measurement_limits: Accuracy is prey-behavior-dependent: evasive prey reduce success to 0.55-0.70. Tail-wind dives are less accurate than headwind dives. The 0.97 is for high-confidence stoops, not all hunting attempts.

scope.definition: Terminal velocity achieved by peregrine falcon in stoop (hunting dive), measured as fraction of aerodynamic theoretical maximum for a streamlined body of equivalent mass and frontal area.

evidence.source: Tucker et al. (1998) 'Curved flight paths and sideways vision in peregrine falcons', Journal of Experimental Biology 201:681-692; Ponitz et al. (2014) peregrine aerodynamics.
cross_domain_examples: peregrine falcon measured at 389 km/h in stoop — fastest recorded animal movement under muscle power
body configuration during stoop: wings swept back, nictitating membrane protects eyes — specialized adaptations
fighter jet terminal velocity in dive 1000 km/h vs 389 km/h peregrine — bird achieves 39% of jet speed at 0.1% the mass

scope.falsifiability: If controlled wind-tunnel measurements show peregrine aerodynamic drag coefficient is not lower than equivalent-mass non-specialized birds in dive posture, the speed advantage is not morphology-driven.
scope.measurement_limits: Terminal velocity depends heavily on dive angle and atmospheric conditions. Ground-level measurement requires radar tracking. The 389 km/h record may be exceptional; typical dives reach 200-300 km/h.

scope.definition: Angular separation between raptor's lateral (temporal) fovea and frontal (central) fovea, enabling simultaneous prey tracking and obstacle avoidance without head movement.

evidence.source: Inzunza et al. (1991) 'Morphology and optics of the tubular eye of the nightjar', Journal of Comparative Neurology; Reymond (1985) 'Spatial visual acuity of the eagle', Vision Research 25:1477-1491.
cross_domain_examples: eagle foveal acuity 2.0-3.6 times human — ~140 cycles/degree vs 60 human — highest known
dual-fovea angle 45° in red-tailed hawk allows prey in peripheral field while central fovea monitors terrain
wide-field military surveillance cameras use multi-sensor fusion to mimic raptor dual-field monitoring

scope.falsifiability: If raptor hunting success is no higher when dual-fovea geometry is preserved vs artificially blocked lateral field, the dual-channel visual strategy provides no behavioral advantage.
scope.measurement_limits: Dual-fovea advantage is greatest during high-speed flight where head turns are aerodynamically costly. Stationary birds use head movements instead. Resolution advantage over mammals degrades in low light.
